name: Scapula Dune
description: Scapula Dune is a world-spanning desert where the sand forms broad, flat plates that overlap like shoulder blades, each one a dune system kilometers across that shifts with agonizing slowness over centuries. Between these plates, deep canyons expose ancient riverbeds and ocean basin sediments that tell of a wetter past. Geothermal vents along the canyon floors provide pockets of warmth and moisture that support small ecosystems in an otherwise arid world.

The heat during the day is oppressive, radiating from the sand in visible waves that distort the horizon into shimmering mirages. At night, the temperature plummets and the desert becomes bitterly cold, the sand contracting with audible clicks and pops. The wind carries fine silicate dust that infiltrates everything, coating surfaces in a gritty film that tastes of metal and dry earth. The sky is a washed-out amber by day, deepening to a star-filled indigo at dusk.

Alien ruins of extraordinary scale emerge periodically from between the dune plates as the sand shifts, only to be buried again decades later. The ruins are built of a stone that does not match any local geology, imported from a source that has not been identified. Monolithic structures stand at the canyon edges, their surfaces carved with astronomical charts that map a sky different from the current one, suggesting they were placed when the planet occupied a different orbital position.

The periodic emergence of the ruins creates a cycle of discovery and loss that drives a persistent archaeological presence on the planet. Desert fauna have adapted to use the ruins as shelter and breeding grounds, creating a complex relationship between the artificial structures and the natural ecosystem. The astronomical charts on the monoliths, if correctly interpreted, could provide information about the planet's orbital history and the identity of the civilization that once considered this desert world important enough to build upon.
